title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Secure Code Generation
authors: Dai, Shih-Chieh; Xu, Jun; Tao, Guanhong
journal: Conference – ICSE '26 (IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering)
keywords: Secure Code Generation, Large Language Models, Vulnerability Detection, Static Analysis, Benchmark Evaluation, Code Functionality
objective: To address flaws in existing evaluation schemes for secure code generation techniques, which assess security and functional correctness independently and rely on a single vulnerability scanner that can miss over 20% of vulnerabilities, by proposing a joint evaluation framework for security and functionality.
type: Empirical/evaluation study (comprehensive comparative study of existing secure code generation techniques); also introduces a new evaluation metric and an enhanced benchmark dataset.
solution: Applies four state-of-the-art secure code generation techniques (SVEN, SafeCoder, CodeGuard+, PromSec) to seven LLMs (CodeLlama, Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, Mistral, StarCoder, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o) and evaluates the generated code on two large datasets (BigCodeBench, SecCodePLT+) using three static analyzers (CodeQL, Bearer, Bandit) and two LLMs (Qwen2.5-72B, Llama3.3-70B) as vulnerability detectors. Introduces a new metric, SAFE@k, which jointly measures security and functionality (weighted by unit-test pass rate), and constructs SecCodePLT+, an enhanced version of SecCodePLT with self-prepared unit tests.
methodology: Uses two datasets (BigCodeBench: 1,140 tasks; SecCodePLT+: 1,201 tasks) covering function-level Python code generation. Applies each secure code generation technique to each base LLM, then evaluates the generated code using three static analyzers and two LLM judges. Introduces the Secure-Pass@k and SAFE@k metrics and performs statistical analysis (t-tests, Cohen's d, two-way ANOVA) comparing base models to secure code generation techniques. Manually inspects 44 sampled cases to validate scanner results and categorize causes of functionality reduction.
findings: CodeQL reports near-100% security for nearly all techniques/models, but Bearer and Bandit report ~25% lower scores, showing scanner results are inconsistent/contradictory; no single scanner covers all vulnerability types. Existing secure code generation techniques improve security to some extent but often at the cost of functional correctness — sometimes degrading base-model functionality by more than 50% (up to 76.74%-84.05% of previously-correct code becoming non-functional), largely by removing vulnerable code or generating irrelevant/'garbage' code. Security improvement is non-monotonic: previously secure code can become insecure after applying these techniques (average 4.11% on BigCodeBench, 6.87% on SecCodePLT+). LLM vulnerability detectors have a high false positive rate (~50%). Under the combined SAFE@k/Secure-Pass@k metrics, most techniques show limited or no real improvement over the base model.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that static analyzers can still produce false negatives even when three are combined, and that the study is limited to Python. Unit tests for SecCodePLT+ were LLM-generated and may not cover all edge cases, and not every experiment was repeated due to high computational cost (~430 GPU-hours per run). The authors also note some construct-validity risk in manual vulnerability judgments, mitigated through multi-author review.
takeaways: Highlights the necessity of evaluating security and functionality jointly rather than separately, and shows that relying on a single vulnerability scanner such as CodeQL is insufficient for reliable assessment. The SAFE@k metric and the 'removed code / garbage code' failure taxonomy offer a more rigorous framework for evaluating secure code generation techniques.
citation: Dai, S.-C., Xu, J., & Tao, G. (2026). Rethinking the evaluation of secure code generation. In 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE '26), April 12-18, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/3744916.3773217

title: SoK: AI Secure Code Generation: Progress, Pitfalls, and Paths Forward
authors: Patir, Rupam; Guo, Keyan; Cai, Haipeng; Hu, Hongxin
keywords: Secure Code Generation, Large Language Models, Systematization of Knowledge, Secure Coding Principles, Vulnerability Evaluation, Benchmarking
objective: To develop a systematic, mechanism-level understanding of how secure code generation interventions, such as prompting, fine-tuning, decoding constraints, and agentic feedback, improve security and why substantial failures persist, moving beyond simple pass/fail evaluation.
type: Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper — combines a systematic literature review/taxonomy with the design of a new measurement framework (KAUGE) and an empirical evaluation using that framework.
solution: Introduces KAUGE (Knowledge-Actuation Unified Gap Evaluation), a three-layer framework built around 'secure coding principles' (SCPs) from OWASP and CERT catalogs: Layer 1 (Knowledge) measures whether models can reason about SCPs in natural language via a 6,382-question NLU benchmark; Layer 2 (Actuation) measures whether models produce functional, exploit-resistant code on executable benchmarks (CWEval, BaxBench); Layer 3 (Gap) uses an exploit-to-SCP defense-formula mapping and an SCP-compliance judge to diagnose why knowledge does or doesn't translate into secure code (four outcomes: principled success, secure by other means, compliant but vulnerable, actuation failure).
methodology: Conducts a systematic literature search (ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, USENIX, DBLP, ACL Anthology, arXiv cs.CR/cs.SE/cs.LG, 2021-2026) with defined inclusion/exclusion criteria and backward/forward snowballing, organizing techniques into four intervention-point families. Builds three constructed artifacts (NLU benchmark, exploit-to-SCP DNF mapping, SCP-compliance judge, each validated against stratified human samples). Evaluates four systems (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, SafeCoder, PurpCodeRL, GPT-5.1-Codex-Mini) plus inference-time interventions (Security-Aware prompting, RCI) and an agentic scaffold (Codex Scaffold) on CWEval (function-level) and BaxBench (application-level) benchmarks, using pass@k, secure-pass@k, and secure@passk metrics; also runs a 10-model robustness check correlating Layer-1 knowledge with Layer-2 actuation.
findings: Secure-coding knowledge (Layer 1) is broadly present across all systems and catalogs, well above chance (lowest score 86.2%); causal reasoning about low-level CERT C/C++ rules is the weakest dimension. Actuation (Layer 2) is far harder than knowledge suggests, and functionality failures (non-runnable code) and exploitable-but-functional code both occur; knowledge correlates with actuation (Spearman rho=0.71, CWEval) but actuation is systematically lower - a benchmark-level knowledge-actuation gap of 47.9 points (CWEval) and 72.9 points (BaxBench). Security fine-tuning (SafeCoder, PurpCodeRL) does not reliably close this gap and can even reduce general implementation competence; agentic scaffolding (Codex Scaffold) is the strongest intervention because it improves software construction, not model knowledge. Layer 3 shows security and SCP-compliance frequently diverge (secure-only 1,100 vs. compliant-only 287 cases, p<.001), revealing distinct failure modes such as 'compliant but vulnerable' code.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that each layer of the KAUGE framework captures only part of the phenomenon: Layer 1 is a fixed-answer NLU proxy, Layer 2 relies on benchmark tests that may miss untested vulnerabilities, and Layer 3's compliance judge is diagnostic rather than ground truth. Results are based on a bounded set of models and benchmarks and are not intended as a comprehensive leaderboard, and reproducibility is limited by evolving commercial APIs and possible data contamination.
takeaways: Establishes that 'knowing' a security principle and 'actuating' it in code are distinct, only loosely coupled capabilities. Recommends that future work focus on translating principles into code through executable feedback, sink-aware guidance, functionality-preserving principle injection, and mechanism-aware evaluation rather than simple pass/fail reporting.
citation: Patir, R., Guo, K., Cai, H., & Hu, H. (2026). SoK: AI secure code generation: Progress, pitfalls, and paths forward. Preprint, University at Buffalo, SUNY. arXiv:2606.25195.

title: Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead
authors: Xin Zhou; Sicong Cao; Xiaobing Sun; David Lo
keywords: LLMs, Vulnerability Detection, Vulnerability Repair, Secure Coding, Prompt Engineering, Fine-tuning, Static Analysis
objective: To systematically review how Large Language Models are applied for software vulnerability detection and repair, categorize existing techniques, identify limitations, and propose future research directions.
type: Systematic Literature Review (SLR)
solution: Reviews 58 studies, classifies LLM adaptation techniques into fine-tuning, prompt engineering and retrieval augmentation for vulnerability detection and repair. Summarizes datasets, deployment strategies, limitations and proposes a future research roadmap.
methodology: Systematic literature review covering 58 papers (2018–2024), classifies LLMs, adaptation techniques, datasets, deployment approaches, identifies research gaps and future roadmap.
findings: Encoder-only LLMs dominate vulnerability detection, while decoder/commercial LLMs are widely used for repair. Fine-tuning is the dominant adaptation technique (≈73% detection, ≈63% repair). The paper highlights major dataset limitations and proposes future research opportunities.
limitations: Survey paper only; does not implement or experimentally evaluate a unified framework. Existing datasets suffer from noisy labels, lack of test cases, and limited deployment into developer workflows.
takeaways: Strong reference for designing SecureCode AI architecture. Supports combining LLMs with static analysis, secure code evaluation, educational feedback, and identifies research gaps that SecureCode AI can address (interactive learning, workflow integration, secure coding assessment).
citation: Xin Zhou, Sicong Cao, Xiaobing Sun, David Lo. Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead. 2024.

title: Guiding AI to Fix Its Own Flaws: An Empirical Study on LLM-Driven Secure Code Generation
authors: Yan, Hao; Vaidya, Swapneel Suhas; Zhang, Xiaokuan; Yao, Ziyu
keywords: Large Language Models, Secure Code Generation, Vulnerability Repair, Prompt Engineering, CWE Classification, Vulnerability Detection
objective: To investigate why large language models often overlook critical security practices and generate insecure code, and to evaluate strategies for guiding LLMs toward secure code generation and repairing the vulnerabilities they introduce.
type: Empirical/evaluation study covering three dimensions of LLM behavior: inherent tendency to generate insecure code, proactive vulnerability prevention, and post-hoc vulnerability repair.
solution: Evaluates a broad range of proprietary and open-weight LLMs (CodeLlama-7B/34B, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.2-3B, StarCoder2-15B, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-16B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o) across three phases: (1) vanilla-prompt code generation to measure inherent vulnerability rate; (2) proactive prevention via self-generated vulnerability hints (LLM lists top-5 likely CWE vulnerabilities for the task, which are then fed back into the generation prompt); (3) post-hoc repair, where CodeQL-detected vulnerabilities are fed back to the LLM either as raw ('direct') feedback or as GPT-4o-generated 'explained' feedback (explanation + suggested fix) for the LLM to repair its own code.
methodology: Uses two Python-focused benchmarks, SecurityEval (121 questions, 69 CWEs) and SecCodePLT (1,071 samples after excluding CodeQL-unsupported CWEs, 21 CWEs). Uses CodeQL as the vulnerability detector throughout. Defines Target Vulnerability Rate (TarV-R) and All Vulnerability Rate (AllV-R) metrics. Evaluates relevance/preciseness of self-generated hints (including manual/GPT-4o-as-judge validation against human annotators), and compares CWE-Definition hints vs. GPT-4o-generated 'contextualized' hints. For repair, manually validates ~160 instances of explained feedback for correctness.
findings: LLMs generate vulnerable code at rates from 9.8% to 42.1% depending on model/benchmark; top-10 vulnerability types largely overlap across models (11 unique types), suggesting shared underlying weaknesses. Self-generated vulnerability hints reduce vulnerabilities only when they are relevant (include the target CWE) and precise (matching official CWE definitions) — imprecise/irrelevant hints can increase vulnerability rates; contextualized hints (grounded in the specific coding scenario) outperform bare CWE definitions, especially for stronger models (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, DeepSeek-Coder-V2). For post-hoc repair, explained feedback (detailed reasoning + suggested fix) yields significantly greater vulnerability reduction than raw/direct CodeQL feedback, particularly for models with strong instruction-following ability (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-Coder-V2, GPT-3.5-turbo); weaker models (e.g., CodeLlama) show little to no improvement from either feedback type.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that evaluation relies solely on CodeQL, a static tool that can miss dynamic or runtime vulnerabilities. The experiments focus exclusively on Python, so findings may not generalize to other languages, and the study is limited to two benchmark datasets that may not cover the full space of vulnerabilities. The evaluation is also static and single-turn, unlike real multi-turn developer-LLM interactions.
takeaways: Demonstrates the importance of hint relevance, precision, and contextualization for effective LLM-based secure coding guidance, and shows that explained, contextualized feedback markedly improves LLM self-repair performance over raw static-analyzer output. Suggests a mixed-model strategy pairing smaller code-optimized models for generation with larger reasoning models for vulnerability explanation and repair.
citation: Yan, H., Vaidya, S. S., Zhang, X., & Yao, Z. (2025). Guiding AI to fix its own flaws: An empirical study on LLM-driven secure code generation. Preprint, George Mason University. arXiv:2506.23034.

title: Secure Coding with AI - From Detection to Repair
authors: Belozerov, Vladislav; Barclay, Peter J.; Sami, Ashkan
keywords: Software Security, LLM, GPT, Static Checkers, Vulnerability Detection, Vulnerability Mitigation
objective: To investigate the security of GPT-generated code obtained from real developer interactions and evaluate the ability of modern Large Language Models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Claude Opus 4.1) to detect and repair security vulnerabilities in practical software development scenarios.
type: Empirical Evaluation / Comparative Experimental Study.
solution: The study extracted GPT-generated C, C++, and C# code from the DevGPT dataset. Source code was first analyzed using static code scanners and manual inspection to identify confirmed vulnerabilities. The vulnerable code was then evaluated using GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Claude Opus 4.1 to detect vulnerabilities, identify CWE IDs, propose fixes, and repair insecure code. The repaired code was manually reviewed and re-scanned to verify remediation.
methodology: The researchers analyzed 2,315 GPT-generated code snippets from the DevGPT dataset. Static scanners and manual inspection identified confirmed vulnerabilities. The vulnerable code was then evaluated using GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and Claude Opus 4.1 for vulnerability detection, CWE classification, and vulnerability repair. Corrected code was manually reviewed and re-scanned. The study also compared results obtained in October 2024 and September 2025 to evaluate improvements in LLM security capabilities over time.
findings: The study identified 56 confirmed vulnerabilities across 48 files. GPT-4.1 correctly detected 46 vulnerabilities and repaired 42, GPT-5 detected 44 and repaired 44, while Claude Opus 4.1 detected 45 and repaired 43. Detection and remediation performance improved substantially compared to earlier experiments, reaching approximately 75-80% accuracy. However, LLM-generated code remained as likely to contain vulnerabilities as developer-written code, and LLMs could confidently provide incorrect security advice.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that although modern LLMs showed improved vulnerability detection and repair capabilities, they still failed to detect or correctly repair all vulnerabilities. Manual code review and static analysis tools remain necessary, as AI models may introduce vulnerabilities or provide misleading security advice.
takeaways: Demonstrates a practical workflow combining static code analysis, manual validation, and LLM-based vulnerability detection and repair using real developer interactions. Shows that detection and remediation performance improved substantially over time, while LLM-generated code remained as likely to contain vulnerabilities as developer-written code.
citation: Belozerov, V., Barclay, P. J., & Sami, A. (2026). Secure Coding with AI - From Detection to Repair. Empirical Software Engineering, 31, Article 93.

title: An Investigation of Quality Issues in Vulnerability Detection Datasets
authors: Yuejun Guo; Seifeddine Bettaieb
keywords: deep learning; software vulnerability detection; dataset quality
objective: Addresses the poor quality of existing datasets used to train deep learning (DL) models for vulnerability detection, which leads to inaccurate, biased, or incomplete detection results.
type: Theoretical framework / analytical study - defines and categorizes dataset quality issues and studies existing datasets; not a tool or intervention.
solution: The paper studies 54 existing vulnerability-detection datasets drawn from 14 reference papers. It defines three critical issues (small sampling size & data imbalance, low coverage of vulnerability types, bias in vulnerability distribution) that cannot be fixed by pre-processing, and three secondary issues (errors in raw data, mislabeling, noisy historical data) that can be addressed through pre-processing. It then proposes good practices for using existing datasets and creating new ones (e.g., data augmentation, weighted loss functions, merging datasets, code refactoring/adversarial attacks to reduce bias).
methodology: Analysis of 27-54 datasets collected from 14 references; sampling-size and imbalance-ratio calculations (#Secure/#Vulnerable); mapping of vulnerability types covered per dataset (Table 2); analysis of vulnerability distribution per dataset (pie charts); case-study examples of mislabeling (e.g., LibPNG cve-2016-10087.c) and noisy historical data (e.g., FFmpeg decode_main_header()).
findings: Except one dataset (FFmpeg by Devign), all studied datasets contain far more secure than vulnerable samples, with an imbalance ratio reaching 325 in the Asterisk dataset. In total, only 28 vulnerability types are covered across all references, and no single reference covers all of them. Noisy historical data (code later found vulnerable but labeled secure) can decrease detection accuracy by over 20%. Mislabeling errors were found even in well-known datasets (e.g., LibPNG).
limitations: Focuses only on defining and cataloguing dataset issues; does not build or evaluate a new detection tool or dataset. Findings are based on 14 references/54 datasets, mostly C/C++ projects, which may not generalize to newer datasets or other languages.
takeaways: Relevant if SecureCode AI ever incorporates ML/DL-based vulnerability detection: highlights the importance of balanced, well-labeled, broad-coverage data and cautions against relying on noisy or imbalanced historical data for automated security evaluation.
citation: Guo, Yuejun, and Seifeddine Bettaieb. "An Investigation of Quality Issues in Vulnerability Detection Datasets." arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.06030 (2024).

title: Benchmarking Software Vulnerability Detection Techniques: A Survey
authors: Yingzhou Bi; Jiangtao Huang; Peihui Liu; Lianmei Wang
keywords: software vulnerability; vulnerability detection; benchmarking; deep learning; survey
objective: Addresses the lack of a comprehensive approach for benchmarking software vulnerability detection techniques, given that many technique papers either skip benchmarking, use non-ground-truth real-world project counts, or use inconsistent datasets/metrics.
type: Theoretical framework / Comprehensive survey - the first survey specifically on vulnerability-detection benchmarking practices, not a new detection technique or tool.
solution: The survey reviews benchmarking practices in (1) technique-proposing papers, split into traditional techniques (static/dynamic/penetration analysis tools such as UNO, CBMC, Frama-C, ITS4, Valgrind, AddressSanitizer, KLEE, evaluated via feature review, case studies on real software like Firefox/Chrome/OpenOffice, or standard suites like SPEC CPU2000/2006 and Juliet Test Suite) and DL-based techniques (e.g., VulDeePecker, SySeVR, Devign, ReVeal, LineVul), analyzed along three dimensions - training/testing data source (synthetic SARD vs. real-world CVE/NVD, and dataset balance), granularity (function-level vs. code-slice vs. statement-level, with/without vulnerability-type classification), and real-world case-study validation (e.g., zero-day detection tests); and (2) third-party empirical studies comparing multiple techniques against ground-truth datasets to compute precision/recall/F1. It then distills 3 core benchmarking challenges (lack of open source/data release, inconsistent evaluation metrics/factors, lack of large-scale real-world datasets) and surveys proposed solutions, including automated/LLM-based vulnerability-injection dataset generation (e.g., VulGen, He & Vechev's LLM-controlled generator).
methodology: Systematic literature survey methodology: separately reviews (a) benchmarking approaches used in papers introducing traditional vs. DL-based vulnerability-detection techniques, and (b) benchmarking approaches used in independent empirical/comparative studies; synthesizes findings into a taxonomy of benchmarking challenges and maps existing/emerging solutions (dataset-quality evaluation, automated vulnerability-dataset generation) to each challenge.
findings: Most synthetic datasets (e.g., SARD-derived) make DL models' results appear inflated versus messier real-world (CVE/NVD) data; real-world vulnerability datasets are inherently imbalanced (e.g., only ~1.46%-9.16% vulnerable samples in TRL/RLMD/ReVeal), making balanced benchmark datasets like Devign unrepresentative of practice; detection granularity is trending finer (function -> slice -> statement level) to better match developer needs; 3 systemic benchmarking challenges persist - lack of released source/data, inconsistent metrics/evaluation factors, and lack of large-scale real-world ground-truthed datasets - with automatic vulnerability-injection/generation (e.g., VulGen, LLM-controlled code generation) emerging as a promising path to scalable, high-quality benchmark data.
limitations: As a survey, it does not itself run new comparative experiments or propose a new benchmark dataset/technique; coverage is necessarily limited to the literature available at time of writing (2023) and may not reflect the newest LLM-based vulnerability-detection benchmarks; conclusions about "best" benchmarking practice are qualitative/synthesized rather than derived from a unified empirical comparison.
takeaways: Provides a directly reusable checklist of what makes vulnerability-detection benchmarking rigorous (ground-truthed real-world data, balanced-vs-realistic tradeoffs, fine-grained statement-level labeling, precision/recall/F1 reporting) that should inform how any AI/GenAI-based secure-coding tool is evaluated, and flags LLM-based synthetic vulnerability-data generation as a candidate technique for building evaluation datasets when real-world labeled data is scarce.
citation: Bi, Yingzhou, Jiangtao Huang, Peihui Liu, and Lianmei Wang. "Benchmarking Software Vulnerability Detection Techniques: A Survey." arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.16362 (2023).

title: Literature review on vulnerability detection using NLP technology
authors: Wu
keywords: Generative AI; Secure Software Coding; Software Security; AI-Driven Development; Cybersecurity; Secure Software Engineering
objective: Examines how Generative AI (GenAI) can strengthen secure coding practices, addressing the gap that AI-driven approaches have not been systematically applied to cybersecurity maturity models for secure software coding.
type: Theoretical framework / Systematic Literature Review (SLR) - synthesizes existing literature; not a tool or intervention.
solution: The paper conducts an SLR following Kitchenham-style guidelines across IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM, SpringerLink and Google Scholar (2694 initial hits narrowed to 31 primary studies via inclusion/exclusion and quality-assessment criteria). It compiles a taxonomy of 109 GenAI practices organized under 10 insecure-coding-practice categories (e.g., automated code analysis, secure coding standards enforcement, threat modeling, dependency scanning, error handling, authentication/authorization, misconfiguration, encryption, XSS, logging/monitoring, race conditions, security testing, supply-chain attacks) and quantifies six GenAI application areas contributing to cybersecurity risk mitigation in software coding (vulnerability detection 27%, secure code generation 23%, threat modeling 17%, real-time monitoring 14%, compliance/code review 12%, malware prevention 7%).
methodology: 8-step SLR process (Planning -> Conducting -> Reporting) per Kitchenham & Charters guidelines: formulate research question (RQ1), develop/validate a search string, search 5 digital libraries, screen by title/abstract/full-text against 5 inclusion and 5 exclusion criteria (Tables 1-2), assess quality via 6 QAC criteria (Table 3), extract qualitative data on GenAI practices, and synthesize into a categorized practice table (Table 4) and a percentage-based role breakdown (Figure 2).
findings: GenAI is most impactful for Automated Vulnerability Detection & Mitigation (27%) and Secure Code Generation & Assistance (23%), together accounting for half of GenAI's contribution to secure coding; Threat Modeling & Predictive Intelligence (17%), Real-time Security Monitoring (14%), Enhanced Compliance & Code Review (12%) and Proactive Malware & Threat Prevention (7%) round out the remaining roles. The review concludes GenAI should be embedded throughout the SDLC rather than treated as an add-on.
limitations: External validity is constrained since the SLR draws from only 31 primary studies (from 2694 initial hits) and industry-specific applicability requires further study; no empirical validation or implementation of the proposed practices is performed; findings rely on secondary literature rather than direct experimentation, so effectiveness of the 109 listed practices is not independently verified.
takeaways: Provides a ready-made taxonomy of 109 concrete GenAI-driven secure-coding practices across 10 vulnerability categories that can seed a checklist or feature list for a GenAI-assisted secure coding tool; the 6-area percentage breakdown (Fig. 2) offers a prioritization signal (vulnerability detection and secure code generation are the highest-value GenAI roles).
citation: Alwageed, Hathal S., and Rafiq Ahmad Khan. "The Role of Generative AI in Strengthening Secure Software Coding Practices: A Systematic Perspective." (2025).

title: Automated Code Assessment for Education: Review, Classification and Perspectives on Techniques and Tools
authors: Combéfis, Sébastien
keywords: Automated Code Assessment, Code Graders, Code Analysis Techniques, Programming Education, Feedback Systems, Static and Dynamic Analysis
objective: To systematically review and classify existing automated code assessment techniques and tools for education, connecting the analyses performed, the feedback produced, and their integration into the learning process.
type: Literature review / survey paper - a systematic review of automated code assessment techniques and tools for education.
solution: Does not present a single tool; instead systematically reviews and classifies ~50 automated code assessment tools/systems (e.g., BOSS, Web-CAT, ArTEMiS, INGInious, CodeMaster, Pythia, GAME, GitGrade, Gradeer, etc.) along: the code/program aspects assessed (syntax, anti-plagiarism, semantic/functional correctness, performance, quality), the methods/techniques used (static, dynamic, hybrid, modelling, AI-based), and the kinds of feedback generated (status, mark, rubric, counterexample, comment, report).
methodology: Conducts an extensive literature search via Google Scholar and publishers (ACM, IEEE, Springer, MDPI) using keywords such as 'automated code assessment', 'automatic code grader', 'automatic programming assessment', and 'automated assessment computer education', supplemented by examining references of found papers. Includes English-language papers published from 2000 onward related to automatic code assessment for educational purposes; papers are categorised into review/survey, tool presentation, and other. Eighteen prior review/survey papers (2005-2021) are analysed to identify six core concerns: code/program aspects assessed, methods/techniques, feedback types, systems/tools developed, integration into the learning process, and quality/impact of assessments - which structure the rest of the paper.
findings: Identifies five hierarchical levels of code aspects typically checked (syntax -> anti-plagiarism -> semantic/functional correctness -> performance -> quality). Static, dynamic, hybrid, modelling, and AI-based (machine learning/neural network/clustering) approaches are the main technique categories, with dynamic/test-based approaches dominating for semantic correctness. Feedback ranges from simple pass/fail status to marks, rubrics, counterexamples, comments, and full reports; more detailed feedback and finer-grained marking granularity are associated with better learner outcomes per cited studies. Automated assessment can support grading, active learning (iterative resubmission), learning-behaviour analytics, and semi-automated (human + automated) assessment. Very little research directly compares the quality of automated versus human/manual grading, and no tool dominates the market; a lack of collaboration/interoperability between platforms is identified as a major structural challenge.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the review could not conclusively determine whether automated code assessment results are as reliable as manual grading, due to insufficient comparative research. The review scope is limited to English-language papers published from 2000 onward, and the authors note limited evidence-based research on AI- and big-data-driven assessment given the relative youth of that sub-area at the time of writing.
takeaways: Provides a reusable taxonomy of code aspects, methods, feedback types, and tools for positioning or designing new automated code assessment systems. Highlights sandboxing as a key design concern given the risk of malicious learner code, and identifies plagiarism detection and cross-platform interoperability as open challenges for the field.
citation: Combéfis, S. (2022). Automated code assessment for education: Review, classification and perspectives on techniques and tools. Software, 1(1), 3-30. https://doi.org/10.3390/software1010002

title: Exploring Automated Code Evaluation Systems and Resources for Code Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey
authors: Md. Mostafizer Rahman; Yutaka Watanobe; Atsushi Shirafuji; Mohamed Hamada
keywords: Automated Code Evaluation System (AES); Online Judge; datasets; Machine Learning; code analysis
objective: Addresses the lack of a comprehensive survey on Automated Code Evaluation Systems (AES)/Online Judges (OJ) and the resources/datasets they generate, which are valuable but under-explored for code-analysis and ML research.
type: Theoretical framework / Comprehensive survey - classifies systems and reviews resources; includes a real-world case study (AOJ) but is not itself an intervention or new tool.
solution: The survey (1) formally defines the AES evaluation method (test instances, solution function, evaluation engine, verdicts such as AC/TLE/MLE/WA/RE, and scoring formulas); (2) classifies AESs into 5 application domains - competitive programming contests, academic/education tools, recruitment & selection, online compilers, and development platforms - with reference tables of real systems (UVa, AOJ, Codeforces, AtCoder, Judge0, LeetCode, etc.); (3) catalogs 26+ benchmark datasets (e.g., CodeNet, CodeContests, BigCloneBench, Devign, HumanEval, CodeXGLUE) and their associated ML coding tasks (defect detection, clone detection, code completion, repair, search, summarization, text-to-code generation, classification); and (4) presents the Aizu Online Judge (AOJ) as a detailed real-world example, covering its hardware architecture (web/database/judge-master/load-balancer/judge-cluster), software architecture (load balancer, broadcaster, judge server internals), operational availability (99.56% uptime 2011-2022), computational performance (~1.1M submissions/year, sub-1-second processing for ~79% of submissions), and its use in published research.
methodology: Literature/system survey methodology: review and classification of AES literature and systems by application domain; compilation of datasets and ML task tables from prior benchmark papers; in-depth technical description and empirical operational-statistics analysis (uptime equations, submission counts, waiting-time distributions 2011-2022) of the AOJ system as an illustrative case study.
findings: AESs serve 5 distinct domains beyond contests (education, recruitment, compilers, development platforms); 26+ open datasets support ML tasks from defect/clone detection to text-to-code generation; the AOJ case study shows the system achieved ~99.56% availability over 12 years, processed over 8 million submissions with growing yearly volume (~1.1M in 2022), and had ~79% of submissions evaluated within 1 second, demonstrating AES resources are both operationally reliable and valuable as large-scale real-world code datasets (e.g., feeding IBM's CodeNet and Google's AlphaCode).
limitations: Being a survey, it does not propose or evaluate a new detection/evaluation technique; the AOJ case study is a single-system example (may not generalize to all OJ platforms); coverage of newer LLM-based code-generation tools is limited since the base article predates the recent surge of large language model coding assistants.
takeaways: Useful as a catalog of datasets (e.g., CodeNet, Devign, CodeXGLUE) and ML coding tasks (vulnerability/defect detection, code repair) that could be reused for benchmarking a secure-coding tool; the AES evaluation-method formalization (test instances, verdicts, scoring) offers a template for how a code-evaluation/security-checking backend could be structured and measured for reliability and performance.
citation: Rahman, Md. Mostafizer, Yutaka Watanobe, Atsushi Shirafuji, and Mohamed Hamada. "Exploring Automated Code Evaluation Systems and Resources for Code Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey." J. ACM 37, no. 4, Article 111 (2018).

title: A Survey on Feedback Types in Automated Programming Assessment Systems
authors: Frankford, Eduard; Antensteiner, Tobias; Vierhauser, Michael; Sauerwein, Clemens; Wallner, Vivien; Groher, Iris; Plösch, Reinhold; Breu, Ruth
journal: Journal – ACM Transactions on Computing Education (in press)
keywords: Automated Programming Assessment, Feedback Types, AI-Generated Feedback, Unit Testing, Programming Education, Student Learning
objective: To investigate how different feedback mechanisms, namely compiler feedback, unit test feedback, and LLM-based feedback, are perceived by students and how effective each is in supporting problem-solving during introductory programming education.
type: Empirical/intervention study — a large-scale mixed-methods experiment (quantitative performance analysis plus qualitative/survey-based perception analysis) comparing three feedback types implemented within an existing APAS.
solution: Implements and compares three feedback types within the Artemis APAS: (1) Compiler Feedback - default compiler output (syntax/runtime errors) only, simulating a minimal-support IDE environment; (2) Traditional Unit Test Feedback - predefined JUnit tests validating correctness against specific test cases, showing pass/fail per test with error locations; (3) AI-Generated Feedback - GPT-3.5-Turbo used as an adaptive 'tutor' via a fixed, non-interactive prompt that gives hints (not full solutions) based on the student's code and the problem statement.
methodology: Uses the Goal Question Metric (GQM) approach to define the research goal, two research questions (perception of feedback types; effect of feedback types on task success), and associated metrics. Combines a TAM (Technology Acceptance Model)-based questionnaire survey (administered after each of three programming exercises: Mars Rover, Array Transformation, Matrix Validation) with quantitative performance analysis (unit test results, submission logs, time between submissions) across 212 students at two universities. Four data collection points: demographics questionnaire, system logs during exercises, post-exercise TAM survey, and a post-experiment open-ended questionnaire (85 respondents). Statistical analysis uses Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Kruskal-Wallis H-tests, and post-hoc Dunn's tests with Bonferroni correction; thematic analysis for open-ended responses.
findings: Students rated Unit Test Feedback highest for quality/usefulness (mean 4.8/7) and most preferred it overall (56%), followed by AI Feedback (26%, mean 4.2/7) and Compiler Feedback least preferred (18%, mean 3.4/7) - all pairwise differences statistically significant. However, on final correctness scores, AI Feedback significantly outperformed both Unit Test Feedback and Compiler Feedback (mean 65.44 vs. 57.52 vs. 41.41); AI Feedback also led to more submission attempts and longer time intervals between submissions, suggesting deeper/more sustained engagement. Some students reported AI Feedback occasionally gave incorrect or 'hallucinated' error messages, particularly once code was mostly correct.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that exercises were limited to array-related topics reviewed by a bounded set of instructors, which may not capture the breadth of programming curricula. AI-guided feedback used only GPT-3.5-Turbo with a fixed, non-interactive prompt, and possible self-selection bias exists since students received bonus points for participation. The sample was drawn mainly from first- and second-year students at two Austrian universities, limiting generalizability.
takeaways: Suggests combining unit tests, valued for reliable correctness verification, with AI-generated feedback, valued for adaptive and exploratory guidance, as a hybrid feedback strategy. Highlights a discrepancy between students' subjective preference for unit tests and their objectively better performance with AI feedback, and flags reliability and hallucination as open challenges for AI-based feedback systems.
citation: Frankford, E., Antensteiner, T., Vierhauser, M., Sauerwein, C., Wallner, V., Groher, I., Plösch, R., & Breu, R. (2025). A survey on feedback types in automated programming assessment systems. ACM Transactions on Computing Education (accepted for publication).

title: An Online Integrated Development Environment for Automated Programming Assessment Systems
authors: Eduard Frankford; Daniel Crazzolara; Michael Vierhauser; Niklas Meißner; Stephan Krusche; Ruth Breu
keywords: Teaching Tools; Automated Programming Assessment Systems; Integrated Development Environments; Artemis; Advanced Learning Technologies
objective: Addresses the lack of feature-rich online code editors (e.g., syntax highlighting, auto-completion, error highlighting, integrated terminal) in Automated Programming Assessment Systems (APASs) compared to traditional desktop IDEs, which can negatively impact the learning experience.
type: Intervention / development exercise - defines requirements and presents a prototypical open-source implementation of a scalable, secure online IDE integrated into the APAS Artemis.
solution: Implements a browser-based online IDE (file browser, code editor, problem statement viewer, terminal) integrated with the Artemis APAS. Uses a Language Server Protocol (LSP) architecture shared across multiple user sessions with load balancing to reduce memory usage; Docker containers isolate each integrated terminal for security; custom debouncing reduces WebSocket message traffic; a 'run' button executes language-specific build/test commands (e.g., mvn clean test, pytest). Supports Java, Python, and C.
methodology: (1) Analysis of state-of-the-art desktop IDEs (VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse) to identify key features. (2) Requirements survey of 48 APAS users across 3 Austrian universities rating importance of IDE features. (3) Prototype design and implementation extending Artemis's native editor with an LSP server and Docker-based terminal. (4) Evaluation via a Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) questionnaire (n=27 students) plus memory-usage benchmarking.
findings: Syntax Highlighting and Syntax Error Highlighting were rated the most important IDE features. Students found the online IDE easy to use and learn, but had mixed/negative views on its utility, effectiveness, and productivity for advanced exercises, preferring desktop IDEs like VSCode/CLion for those. Debouncing reduced messages sent by ~43% without harming user experience. Memory usage grew linearly (~130MB per additional user, 53MB to 650MB for 0-5 users), and connecting multiple sessions to one LSP server plus load balancing roughly halved memory use versus a full Theia IDE container (~260MB).
limitations: Integration and evaluation were exclusive to the Artemis platform, limiting generalizability, though the underlying LSP/Docker architecture is described as platform-agnostic. The evaluation sample was small (27 students from a single introductory course). Students found the editor less suitable for advanced exercises.
takeaways: Directly relevant to SecureCode AI's planned Online Code Editor: demonstrates practical architecture choices (LSP with load balancing, debouncing, Docker-sandboxed terminals for security) for building a scalable, resource-efficient, secure browser-based code editor supporting Java/Python.

title: From Preventive to Reactive: How AI Coding Assistants Transform Developers' Security Awareness
authors: Faisal Haque Bappy; Tahrim Hossain; Sidratul Muntaher Meheraj; Annoor Sharara Akhand; Tasfia Tabassum; Tarannum Shaila Zaman; Raiful Hasan; Tariqul Islam
journal: USENIX Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS)
keywords: AI coding assistants; secure coding; security awareness; developer behavior; trust calibration; qualitative study
objective: Investigates how AI coding assistants (e.g., GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) transform professional developers' security awareness in authentic practice, and whether this differs by developers' exposure to AI during professional formation.
type: Intervention/empirical study - mixed-methods qualitative study (semi-structured interviews + observed Think-Aloud coding sessions), not a tool-building paper.
solution: 15 professional software engineers, grouped into 3 AI-exposure cohorts (Pre-AI, AI-era, AI-native, cutoffs pre-2022/2022-2023/2024-onward), completed a 45-60 min session: (1) a semi-structured interview on security practices and AI tool use, followed by (2) a Think-Aloud coding task using Gemini CLI with Gemini 2.5 Pro inside a self-hosted VS Code Server, choosing among 3 tasks - feature implementation (/update-profile endpoint), project initialization (backend scaffold + /health endpoint), or debugging a concurrency/race-condition file-upload bug. Data were analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis (interview codebook of 20 codes/6 categories) and structured coding-session observation (prompting strategy, security-relevant decisions, task completion approach).
methodology: Mixed-methods design: semi-structured interview guide (Appendix B, background -> AI usage/trust -> security practices -> task reflection) followed by a Think-Aloud coding session on one of 3 realistic, security-relevant tasks with no explicit security requirements stated (Appendix C); screen recordings and code artifacts were analyzed for prompting/iteration patterns, security-relevant decisions, and task completion approach, triangulated against interview responses; thematic saturation reached at ~13 of 15 participants.
findings: None of the 14 participants who coded included security requirements in their initial prompts, even when they had just articulated relevant vulnerabilities in the interview (the "prompting gap"); only 2 of 14 caught unstated security issues unprompted; experience/AI-exposure cohort did not reliably predict security performance; developers independently invented coping strategies (restricting agent permissions, security-oriented prompt templates, post-implementation "any security concerns?" queries) that are unsupported by current tools/organizations; AI coding assistants shift security thinking from the authorship (preventive) phase to the review (reactive) phase.
limitations: Small, male-skewed sample (N=15), limiting generalizability; interview-first design may have primed security reflection before coding (though priming effect appears minimal since most still omitted security); used only Gemini CLI/Gemini 2.5 Pro, which may not represent other AI-native tools (e.g., Claude Code, Copilot); the Think-Aloud setting may have induced atypical deliberateness versus routine work.
takeaways: Directly actionable for a "SecureCode AI"-type project: motivates building security into the generation workflow by default (since users rarely prompt for it), suggests trust-calibration UI cues (differentiating boilerplate vs. security-sensitive code), and supports formalizing developer-invented coping strategies (e.g., a mandatory post-generation "security concerns?" pass, permission-scoped agents) as first-class product features rather than relying on individual initiative.

"From Preventive to Reactive: How AI Coding Assistants Transform Developers' Security Awareness." USENIX Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS) (2026).

title: Towards a Success Model for Automated Programming Assessment Systems Used as a Formative Assessment Tool
authors: Clemens Sauerwein; Tobias Antensteiner; Stefan Oppl; Iris Groher; Alexander Meschtscherjakov; Philipp Zech; Ruth Breu
journal: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V.1 (ITiCSE 2023), ACM
keywords: Automated Assessment Tool; Automated Programming Assessment System; Success Model; User Satisfaction; Empirical Study; Survey; Programming Education
objective: Addresses the lack of a common understanding, in research and practice, of the factors that drive the success (student satisfaction) of Automated Programming Assessment Systems (APASs), and the unexamined role of mediating constructs.
type: Theoretical framework with empirical validation - devises and statistically validates a success model via a large-scale student survey (PLS-SEM), not a software tool.
solution: Builds a success model for APASs combining DeLone & McLean's IS Success Model with Zhang & Dang's Blended Learning Success Model. Four exogenous constructs (Motivation, Information Quality, System Quality, Service Quality) act through three mediator constructs (Learning Climate, Blended Learning Flexibility, Task-Technology Fit) to influence the endogenous construct Satisfaction. Validated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with the R SEMinR package.
methodology: Research model derived from DeLone & McLean and Zhang & Dang; 30-item Likert-scale questionnaire (LimeSurvey) covering MOT, INQ, SYQ, SEQ, LEC, BLF, TTF, SAT; 414 students surveyed (368 valid responses after removing incomplete ones); measurement and structural model evaluated (indicator reliability, internal consistency, AVE, HTMT, VIF); path coefficients tested via bootstrapping (10,000 resamples); mediation analysis per Cepeda Carrion et al./Baron & Kenny.
findings: Motivation, Information Quality, and System Quality each have a significant indirect effect on Satisfaction through Learning Climate, Blended Learning Flexibility, and Task-Technology Fit. Service Quality's effect on Learning Climate and Blended Learning Flexibility was not significant. Motivation's effect on Satisfaction is fully mediated by the three mediators; Information Quality's and System Quality's effects are partially mediated.
limitations: Possible selection bias (only CS-related students voluntarily participated, likely high computer affinity). Findings are based on a single APAS (Artemis), though basic APAS functionality is argued to be similar across systems. Several constructs (MOT, INQ, SYQ, TTF) were measured only at an abstract level. Teaching format was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic (remote instead of face-to-face).
takeaways: Useful for SecureCode AI's Progress Dashboard/Feedback/Leaderboard design: indicates that system quality (reliability, flexibility, sufficient functions), information quality (relevant, accurate, understandable feedback), and motivation (e.g., gamification) are the constructs most likely to drive learner satisfaction, mediated by enjoyment, flexibility, and fit with learning needs.

"Towards a Success Model for Automated Programming Assessment Systems Used as a Formative Assessment Tool." In Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2023), pp. 1-7. ACM, 2023.

title: Using an LLM to Help With Code Understanding
authors: Nam et al.
keywords: University Education; Bug Bounty; Cybersecurity Specialization; Secure coding; Course Assignment; Experience Report
objective: Addresses the shortage of practical, hands-on ethical-hacking/cybersecurity education by proposing and evaluating the integration of real-world Bug Bounty Programs (BBPs) into a university secure coding course curriculum.
type: Intervention / Development exercise - a pedagogical intervention (optional course-project track) evaluated via an experience-report / mixed quantitative-qualitative study, not a technical tool.
solution: Within an existing Master's-level secure coding course (project worth ~half the final grade, normally Tutorial/Implementation/Original-work tracks), the authors added a voluntary 4th "Bug Bounty Challenge" (BBCh) track: students select and register for a real BBP (e.g., T-Mobile, HackerOne-hosted Shopify/Epic Games/Boozt, TryHackMe, HackTheBox, Coinbase), attend an optional expert-delivered lecture on ethical-hacking methodology/legal framework/reporting, spend ~40-60 recommended hours attempting to find and responsibly report a vulnerability, and submit a technical report/paper plus oral presentation; grading is based on process/tools/report quality, not on whether a vulnerability was actually found.
methodology: Quasi-experimental course-based evaluation: 38 students enrolled in the semester project, 19 opted into the BBCh track (13 completed it, 12 completed a follow-up survey); mixed quantitative (Likert-scale questionnaires on technical work, self-evaluation, project evaluation) and qualitative (analysis of submitted project reports) methods; data collected anonymously with university ethics/course-supervisor approval.
findings: BBCh project scores (avg. 40/49) were comparable to the other three traditional project types (avg. 39/49), i.e., no added difficulty penalty; 2 of 13 completing students found real vulnerabilities (an unreported IDOR and a reported CSRF + redirect-validation flaw); self-rated ethical-hacking understanding rose from 1.92 to 3.58 (of 5); interest in a cybersecurity career rose from 41.7% to 50%; project enjoyability rated 4.16/5 vs. regular projects, and 83% of students planned to continue with bug bounty activity afterward; most-used learning resources were PortSwigger Academy (8) and video tutorials (5).
limitations: Single-course, single-run experiment (small n=12-19 in the BBCh track), limiting generalizability; success depended heavily on students choosing a familiar system to test; risk factors (finding nothing, violating BBP rules) were mitigated but not eliminated by the optional lecture; no control group directly comparing security-outcome skill gains against a non-BBP secure-coding assignment.
takeaways: Offers a validated pedagogical model (voluntary, process-graded, real-world BBP track) that could inform training/curriculum recommendations in a broader secure-coding education strategy; the finding that grading progress/process rather than success avoids penalizing students while still producing measurable awareness/skill gains is a transferable design principle for any secure-coding training program (including AI-assisted coding training).
citation: Malinka, Kamil, Anton Firc, Pavel Loutocký, Jakub Vostoupal, Andrej Krištofík, and František Kasl. "Using Real-world Bug Bounty Programs in Secure Coding Course: Experience Report." arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.12043 (2024).

title: The Role of Generative AI in Strengthening Secure Software Coding Practices: A Systematic Perspective
authors: Alwageed, Hathal S.; Khan, Rafiq Ahmad
keywords: Generative AI, Secure Software Coding, Software Security, AI-Driven Development, Cybersecurity, Secure Software Engineering.
objective: To systematically investigate the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on secure software coding by examining its benefits, challenges, cybersecurity implications, and future directions. The study aims to understand how AI-driven code generation tools help mitigate security risks, support secure coding standards, and improve software development efficiency.
type: Systematic Literature Review (SLR).
solution: The study follows a Systematic Literature Review methodology by defining research questions, developing search strings, searching multiple digital libraries, applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, performing quality assessment, and synthesizing existing studies related to Generative AI for secure software coding. It reviews AI frameworks, secure coding practices, cybersecurity risks, AI models, and maturity models to identify current practices and future research opportunities.
methodology: The research employed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR). Search queries were executed across IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. Studies were screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, followed by quality assessment. Out of 2,694 retrieved studies, 31 primary studies were selected for detailed analysis. The review synthesized qualitative and quantitative information on GenAI practices for secure software coding.
findings: The review found that Generative AI can enhance secure software coding by improving vulnerability detection, supporting secure coding standards, mitigating cybersecurity risks, and increasing software development efficiency. Effective adoption requires integration with AI frameworks, governance mechanisms, organizational readiness, workforce preparation, and explainability mechanisms.
limitations: The authors acknowledge limited research on applying AI-driven approaches to cybersecurity maturity models for secure software coding, and highlight ongoing challenges related to organizational readiness, ethical AI adoption, governance, explainability, and workforce preparation.
takeaways: Provides a comprehensive overview of current generative AI approaches, cybersecurity challenges, and research gaps in secure software coding, and shows that effective adoption requires integration with AI frameworks, governance mechanisms, and workforce preparation alongside technical improvements.
citation: Alwageed, H. S., & Khan, R. A. (2025). The Role of Generative AI in Strengthening Secure Software Coding Practices: A Systematic Perspective.

title: The Role of Generative AI in Strengthening Secure Software Coding Practices: A Systematic Perspective
authors: Hathal S. Alwageed; Rafiq Ahmad Khan
keywords: Generative AI; Secure Software Coding; Software Security; AI-Driven Development; Cybersecurity; Secure Software Engineering
objective: Examines how Generative AI (GenAI) can strengthen secure coding practices, addressing the gap that AI-driven approaches have not been systematically applied to cybersecurity maturity models for secure software coding.
type: Theoretical framework / Systematic Literature Review (SLR) - synthesizes existing literature; not a tool or intervention.
solution: The paper conducts an SLR following Kitchenham-style guidelines across IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, ACM, SpringerLink and Google Scholar (2694 initial hits narrowed to 31 primary studies via inclusion/exclusion and quality-assessment criteria). It compiles a taxonomy of 109 GenAI practices organized under 10 insecure-coding-practice categories (e.g., automated code analysis, secure coding standards enforcement, threat modeling, dependency scanning, error handling, authentication/authorization, misconfiguration, encryption, XSS, logging/monitoring, race conditions, security testing, supply-chain attacks) and quantifies six GenAI application areas contributing to cybersecurity risk mitigation in software coding (vulnerability detection 27%, secure code generation 23%, threat modeling 17%, real-time monitoring 14%, compliance/code review 12%, malware prevention 7%).
methodology: 8-step SLR process (Planning -> Conducting -> Reporting) per Kitchenham & Charters guidelines: formulate research question (RQ1), develop/validate a search string, search 5 digital libraries, screen by title/abstract/full-text against 5 inclusion and 5 exclusion criteria (Tables 1-2), assess quality via 6 QAC criteria (Table 3), extract qualitative data on GenAI practices, and synthesize into a categorized practice table (Table 4) and a percentage-based role breakdown (Figure 2).
findings: GenAI is most impactful for Automated Vulnerability Detection & Mitigation (27%) and Secure Code Generation & Assistance (23%), together accounting for half of GenAI's contribution to secure coding; Threat Modeling & Predictive Intelligence (17%), Real-time Security Monitoring (14%), Enhanced Compliance & Code Review (12%) and Proactive Malware & Threat Prevention (7%) round out the remaining roles. The review concludes GenAI should be embedded throughout the SDLC rather than treated as an add-on.
limitations: External validity is constrained since the SLR draws from only 31 primary studies (from 2694 initial hits) and industry-specific applicability requires further study; no empirical validation or implementation of the proposed practices is performed; findings rely on secondary literature rather than direct experimentation, so effectiveness of the 109 listed practices is not independently verified.
takeaways: Provides a ready-made taxonomy of 109 concrete GenAI-driven secure-coding practices across 10 vulnerability categories that can seed a checklist or feature list for a GenAI-assisted secure coding tool; the 6-area percentage breakdown (Fig. 2) offers a prioritization signal (vulnerability detection and secure code generation are the highest-value GenAI roles).
citation: Alwageed, Hathal S., and Rafiq Ahmad Khan. "The Role of Generative AI in Strengthening Secure Software Coding Practices: A Systematic Perspective." (2025).

title: Enabling Secure Coding: Exploring GenAI for Developer Training and Education
authors: Amburi, Sathwik; Gasiba, Tiago Espinha; Lechner, Ulrike; Pinto-Albuquerque, Maria
keywords: Secure Coding, Industry, Software Development, Generative AI, Large Language Models, Teaching.
objective: To investigate how Generative AI can support secure coding by developing an AI Secure Coding platform that integrates a GPT-4 based chatbot into secure coding challenges. The study aims to understand how developers use GenAI to identify and remediate vulnerabilities and to evaluate developers' opinions on AI-assisted secure coding.
type: Platform Development with Empirical Evaluation (Design Science Research).
solution: The proposed AI Secure Coding Platform provides an interactive secure coding training environment where developers solve AI-generated secure coding challenges. Participants first review vulnerable code, identify vulnerabilities, request AI assistance through a GPT-4 chatbot, refine their findings using AI feedback, and finally submit secure patches. The chatbot can access source code and review comments, suggest mitigations, generate secure patches, explain security concepts, and log all participant interactions.
methodology: The study follows Design Science Research (DSR). An AI Secure Coding platform was designed and evaluated through one DSR cycle. Eighteen industry developers completed three secure coding challenges by identifying vulnerabilities, interacting with the GPT-4 chatbot, refining their findings, fixing vulnerabilities, and completing a post-study survey evaluating their experience with AI-assisted secure coding.
findings: AI assistance increased developer productivity, reduced errors, and helped identify additional vulnerabilities when used as a "second pair of eyes." However, the study also found a risk of developer over-reliance on AI. The proposed platform demonstrates that embedding GenAI into structured secure coding workflows can improve secure coding training while highlighting the need for responsible AI usage.
limitations: The study reports preliminary findings from an initial Design Science Research cycle involving only 18 industry developers, and notes that the platform is still under iterative development, with additional research required to further evaluate its effectiveness.
takeaways: Demonstrates how an AI-powered secure coding platform can combine vulnerability identification, AI-assisted guidance, secure patch generation, and developer training within a structured challenge-based workflow. Highlights both the productivity benefits of AI assistance and the risk of developer over-reliance on AI feedback.
citation: Amburi, S., Gasiba, T. E., Lechner, U., & Pinto-Albuquerque, M. (2025). Enabling Secure Coding: Exploring GenAI for Developer Training and Education. 6th International Computer Programming Education Conference (ICPEC 2025), OpenAccess Series in Informatics (OASIcs).

title: A Systematic Mapping Study on Teaching of Security Concepts in Programming Courses
authors: Alina Torbunova; Adnan Ashraf; Ivan Porres
keywords: systematic mapping study; cybersecurity; secure programming; teaching; university
objective: Addresses the absence of a systematic study on how cybersecurity concepts are taught within programming courses in higher education, and aims to identify security concepts covered, contributions, frameworks, programming environments, and evaluation approaches used.
type: Systematic Mapping Study (literature review) - a theoretical/analytical study, not an intervention or tool.
solution: No tool is built. The study follows established SMS guidelines (Kitchenham & Charters; Petersen et al.), searching six digital libraries (IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Wiley, Web of Science) with a PICOC-derived search string, screening titles/abstracts and full texts, and performing backward/forward snowball sampling and quality assessment to select 24 publications (2010-2023), which are then classified against six research questions (security concepts covered, study program/course level, contribution type, theoretical frameworks used, programming environments, evaluation methods).
methodology: PICOC-based search string across 6 databases (642 initial hits) -> deduplication (484) -> title/abstract screening (85) -> full-text screening (24) -> backward and forward snowball sampling (30 -> 44) -> quality assessment against 6 criteria (24 final studies); two researchers independently screened and coded, resolving disagreements in meetings; data extracted per study against 6 research questions.
findings: Most studies address undergraduate, introductory Computer Science courses. 'Course Modules' is the most common contribution type. OWASP Top 10 is the most-used security framework, followed by ACM Curriculum Guidelines. Java is the most-used programming language; Python appears in only one study. Post-surveys are the most common evaluation method, but these do not assess actual student knowledge/skill. 14 of 24 studies cover all three security knowledge categories (security issues, negative impacts, countermeasures); injection flaws (including SQL injection and XSS) are among the most frequently covered vulnerability topics.
limitations: SpringerLink was excluded from the search due to database limitations. Only 24 studies met the inclusion/quality criteria, which may not capture all relevant work. The study identifies gaps and opportunities (advanced courses, holistic frameworks, Python coverage) but does not resolve them itself.
takeaways: Strongly validates SecureCode AI's research gap: confirms that hands-on, practical secure-coding platforms combining automated evaluation with instructional feedback are underrepresented; supports focusing first on Injection Attacks (SQL injection/XSS are commonly taught); supports using OWASP as the guiding framework; and highlights that most existing work is evaluated only via post-surveys rather than actual code/coding-skill assessment, reinforcing SecureCode AI's approach of automated functional + security evaluation.
citation: Torbunova, Alina, Adnan Ashraf, and Ivan Porres. "A Systematic Mapping Study on Teaching of Security Concepts in Programming Courses." arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.07511 (2024).
