findings: BBCh project scores (avg. 40/49) were comparable to the other three traditional project types (avg. 39/49), i.e., no added difficulty penalty; 2 of 13 completing students found real vulnerabilities (an unreported IDOR and a reported CSRF + redirect-validation flaw); self-rated ethical-hacking understanding rose from 1.92 to 3.58 (of 5); interest in a cybersecurity career rose from 41.7% to 50%; project enjoyability rated 4.16/5 vs. regular projects, and 83% of students planned to continue with bug bounty activity afterward; most-used learning resources were PortSwigger Academy (8) and video tutorials (5).
limitations: Single-course, single-run experiment (small n=12-19 in the BBCh track), limiting generalizability; success depended heavily on students choosing a familiar system to test; risk factors (finding nothing, violating BBP rules) were mitigated but not eliminated by the optional lecture; no control group directly comparing security-outcome skill gains against a non-BBP secure-coding assignment.
takeaways: Offers a validated pedagogical model (voluntary, process-graded, real-world BBP track) that could inform training/curriculum recommendations in a broader secure-coding education strategy; the finding that grading progress/process rather than success avoids penalizing students while still producing measurable awareness/skill gains is a transferable design principle for any secure-coding training program (including AI-assisted coding training).
citation: Malinka, Kamil, Anton Firc, Pavel Loutocký, Jakub Vostoupal, Andrej Krištofík, and František Kasl. "Using Real-world Bug Bounty Programs in Secure Coding Course: Experience Report." arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.12043 (2024).

title: Design of Secure Coding Challenges for Cybersecurity Education in the Industry
authors: Tiago Gasiba; Ulrike Lechner; Maria Pinto-Albuquerque; Alae Zouitni
keywords: education; teaching; training; secure coding; industry; cybersecurity; capture-the-flag; game analysis; game design; cybersecurity challenge
objective: Addresses the lack of properly designed defensive Capture-the-Flag (CTF) challenges geared towards software developers in industry, investigating which challenge types are adequate to improve developers' secure coding ability.
type: Intervention / development exercise - a design study that proposes and validates a challenge structure and challenge types through surveys and interviews with industry security experts.
solution: Proposes a three-phase CTF challenge structure (Introduction, Challenge & Logic, Conclusion) with hints and penalties, and six challenge types: Single Choice Question, Multiple Choice Question, Text Entry Challenge, Code Snippet Challenge, Code Entry Challenge, and Associate Left-Right. The design was derived through a preliminary design, a two-part (pre/post) survey, and semi-structured interviews with security experts, then adapted based on majority-agreed feedback.
methodology: Preliminary design based on informal discussions with one security expert -> two-phase survey (pre-survey and post-survey) developed and reviewed by three cybersecurity experts -> one-hour semi-structured interviews with 20 industry security experts (avg. 4 years' experience) -> manual coding of open-ended responses by three experts -> adaptation of design based on changes agreed by >2/3 of participants -> final challenge structure and types.
findings: Code-Entry-Challenge and Code-Snippet-Challenge received the highest agreement (mean 4.30 on a 5-point Likert scale) as suitable challenge types; Text-Entry-Challenge was least preferred (mean 3.15). 80% of experts favored using hints, especially for difficult challenges, ideally disclosing key concepts or external references. 60% favored penalties, particularly for hint use (65%).
limitations: Based on a limited number of participants (20 experts) from a specific company background, threatening generalizability. Feedback came only from security experts, not from real CTF/developer players. No systematic literature review was performed to source prior work.
takeaways: Directly relevant to SecureCode AI's challenge design: the Code-Entry-Challenge and Code-Snippet-Challenge types map closely to the planned 'Fix Vulnerability' and 'Write Secure Code' challenge types, and the proposed hint/penalty and three-phase (intro/challenge/conclusion+feedback) structure can inform SecureCode AI's challenge and feedback flow.
citation: Gasiba, Tiago, Ulrike Lechner, Maria Pinto-Albuquerque, and Alae Zouitni. "Design of Secure Coding Challenges for Cybersecurity Education in the Industry." arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.02108 (2021).

title: Cybersecurity Games for Secure Programming Education in the Industry
authors: Gasiba et al.
keywords: software vulnerability; vulnerability detection; benchmarking; deep learning; survey
objective: Addresses the lack of a comprehensive approach for benchmarking software vulnerability detection techniques, given that many technique papers either skip benchmarking, use non-ground-truth real-world project counts, or use inconsistent datasets/metrics.
type: Theoretical framework / Comprehensive survey - the first survey specifically on vulnerability-detection benchmarking practices, not a new detection technique or tool.
solution: The survey reviews benchmarking practices in (1) technique-proposing papers, split into traditional techniques (static/dynamic/penetration analysis tools such as UNO, CBMC, Frama-C, ITS4, Valgrind, AddressSanitizer, KLEE, evaluated via feature review, case studies on real software like Firefox/Chrome/OpenOffice, or standard suites like SPEC CPU2000/2006 and Juliet Test Suite) and DL-based techniques (e.g., VulDeePecker, SySeVR, Devign, ReVeal, LineVul), analyzed along three dimensions - training/testing data source (synthetic SARD vs. real-world CVE/NVD, and dataset balance), granularity (function-level vs. code-slice vs. statement-level, with/without vulnerability-type classification), and real-world case-study validation (e.g., zero-day detection tests); and (2) third-party empirical studies comparing multiple techniques against ground-truth datasets to compute precision/recall/F1. It then distills 3 core benchmarking challenges (lack of open source/data release, inconsistent evaluation metrics/factors, lack of large-scale real-world datasets) and surveys proposed solutions, including automated/LLM-based vulnerability-injection dataset generation (e.g., VulGen, He & Vechev's LLM-controlled generator).
methodology: Systematic literature survey methodology: separately reviews (a) benchmarking approaches used in papers introducing traditional vs. DL-based vulnerability-detection techniques, and (b) benchmarking approaches used in independent empirical/comparative studies; synthesizes findings into a taxonomy of benchmarking challenges and maps existing/emerging solutions (dataset-quality evaluation, automated vulnerability-dataset generation) to each challenge.
findings: Most synthetic datasets (e.g., SARD-derived) make DL models' results appear inflated versus messier real-world (CVE/NVD) data; real-world vulnerability datasets are inherently imbalanced (e.g., only ~1.46%-9.16% vulnerable samples in TRL/RLMD/ReVeal), making balanced benchmark datasets like Devign unrepresentative of practice; detection granularity is trending finer (function -> slice -> statement level) to better match developer needs; 3 systemic benchmarking challenges persist - lack of released source/data, inconsistent metrics/evaluation factors, and lack of large-scale real-world ground-truthed datasets - with automatic vulnerability-injection/generation (e.g., VulGen, LLM-controlled code generation) emerging as a promising path to scalable, high-quality benchmark data.
limitations: As a survey, it does not itself run new comparative experiments or propose a new benchmark dataset/technique; coverage is necessarily limited to the literature available at time of writing (2023) and may not reflect the newest LLM-based vulnerability-detection benchmarks; conclusions about "best" benchmarking practice are qualitative/synthesized rather than derived from a unified empirical comparison.
takeaways: Provides a directly reusable checklist of what makes vulnerability-detection benchmarking rigorous (ground-truthed real-world data, balanced-vs-realistic tradeoffs, fine-grained statement-level labeling, precision/recall/F1 reporting) that should inform how any AI/GenAI-based secure-coding tool is evaluated, and flags LLM-based synthetic vulnerability-data generation as a candidate technique for building evaluation datasets when real-world labeled data is scarce.
citation: Bi, Yingzhou, Jiangtao Huang, Peihui Liu, and Lianmei Wang. "Benchmarking Software Vulnerability Detection Techniques: A Survey." arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.16362 (2023).

title: Securing Web Apps with ChatGPT: A Teaching Plan for Undergraduate Students
authors: Nocera, Sabato; Romano, Simone; Francese, Rita; Casertano, Francesco; Scanniello, Giuseppe
journal: Journal – The Journal of Systems & Software
keywords: Software engineering education, Teaching secure development, Software vulnerabilities, Generative artificial intelligence, Large language models, ChatGPT
objective: To design, enact, and evaluate a teaching plan that integrates ChatGPT into undergraduate Computer Science education to help students identify and fix vulnerabilities in e-commerce web applications while understanding both the opportunities and limitations of LLMs in secure web development.
type: Educational Experience Report / Teaching Intervention.
solution: The teaching plan integrates industrial lectures, academic instruction, laboratory exercises, and homework assignments. Students learn secure software development through vulnerability identification and fixing tasks on e-commerce web applications using ChatGPT support. The intervention includes practitioner-led sessions, academic lectures on vulnerability fixing with and without ChatGPT, controlled laboratory assignments, and homework activities.
methodology: The teaching plan was implemented in an undergraduate web technologies course involving 105 students. It consisted of: (1) vulnerability identification and exploitation session by industry practitioners, (2) secure software development lecture by practitioners, (3) academic lecture on fixing vulnerabilities with and without ChatGPT, (4) laboratory assignment under controlled conditions, and (5) homework assignment using ChatGPT. Student performance and perceptions were evaluated throughout the teaching activities.
findings: Students supported by ChatGPT fixed significantly more vulnerabilities than students without AI support. However, ChatGPT also led to some incorrect fixes. Students perceived vulnerability fixing as easier when using ChatGPT, and most participants reported improved knowledge of secure web development and positive learning experiences.
limitations: The authors report that ChatGPT can generate incorrect vulnerability fixes for certain types of vulnerabilities, and emphasize that it should be treated as a support tool rather than a complete solution, requiring critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs.
takeaways: Demonstrates the integration of ChatGPT into secure web development education through structured vulnerability identification and remediation exercises while emphasizing the need for human validation of AI-generated solutions.
citation: Nocera, S., Romano, S., Francese, R., Casertano, F., & Scanniello, G. (2026). Securing Web Apps with ChatGPT: A Teaching Plan for Undergraduate Students. The Journal of Systems & Software, 241, 112971.

title: Is Secure Coding Education in the Industry Needed? An Investigation Through a Large Scale Survey
authors: Gasiba, Tiago Espinha; Lechner, Ulrike; Pinto-Albuquerque, Maria; Mendez, Daniel
keywords: Education, Training, Secure Coding Guidelines, Software Developers, Awareness, Survey
objective: To investigate whether secure coding education is needed in industry by examining software developers' awareness of secure coding guidelines, their compliance with these guidelines, and the factors influencing compliance. The study also aims to provide actionable recommendations for improving secure coding education in industry.
type: Large-Scale Empirical Survey Study.
solution: The researchers designed and deployed a large-scale survey based on four established theories: IT Security Policy Compliance, Neutralization Theory, Security-Related Stress, and IT Security Awareness. The survey collected demographic information, secure coding awareness, compliance behaviour, and background information from industrial software developers. The collected data were analyzed to identify factors influencing secure coding awareness, compliance, and the need for secure coding education.
methodology: A large-scale survey was conducted with 194 industrial software developers over seven months. The survey investigated awareness, compliance, and educational needs related to secure coding guidelines. It was based on four theoretical frameworks: IT Security Policy Compliance, Neutralization Theory, Security-Related Stress, and IT Security Awareness. The researchers analyzed responses to answer three research questions related to compliance factors, awareness, and the necessity of secure coding education.
findings: The survey demonstrated a clear need for secure coding education in industry. It identified factors influencing developers' compliance with secure coding guidelines, evaluated their level of awareness, and produced 15 actionable recommendations for improving secure coding education and awareness within software organizations. The study also made the survey dataset publicly available for future research.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the study focuses specifically on industrial software developers and secure coding guidelines, and is survey-based, measuring developers' awareness and perceptions rather than experimentally evaluating secure coding performance or educational interventions.
takeaways: Provides evidence that developer awareness and education are essential for reducing software vulnerabilities in industry. Supports the importance of secure coding training, awareness assessment, and compliance evaluation as foundations for effective secure coding education programs.
citation: Gasiba, T. E., Lechner, U., Pinto-Albuquerque, M., & Mendez, D. (2021). Is Secure Coding Education in the Industry Needed? An Investigation Through a Large Scale Survey. arXiv Preprint.

title: Cyber security enhancements with reinforcement learning: A zero-day vulnerability identification perspective
authors: Naeem et al.
keywords: Automated Code Evaluation System (AES); Online Judge; datasets; Machine Learning; code analysis
objective: Addresses the lack of a comprehensive survey on Automated Code Evaluation Systems (AES)/Online Judges (OJ) and the resources/datasets they generate, which are valuable but under-explored for code-analysis and ML research.
type: Theoretical framework / Comprehensive survey - classifies systems and reviews resources; includes a real-world case study (AOJ) but is not itself an intervention or new tool.
solution: The survey (1) formally defines the AES evaluation method (test instances, solution function, evaluation engine, verdicts such as AC/TLE/MLE/WA/RE, and scoring formulas); (2) classifies AESs into 5 application domains - competitive programming contests, academic/education tools, recruitment & selection, online compilers, and development platforms - with reference tables of real systems (UVa, AOJ, Codeforces, AtCoder, Judge0, LeetCode, etc.); (3) catalogs 26+ benchmark datasets (e.g., CodeNet, CodeContests, BigCloneBench, Devign, HumanEval, CodeXGLUE) and their associated ML coding tasks (defect detection, clone detection, code completion, repair, search, summarization, text-to-code generation, classification); and (4) presents the Aizu Online Judge (AOJ) as a detailed real-world example, covering its hardware architecture (web/database/judge-master/load-balancer/judge-cluster), software architecture (load balancer, broadcaster, judge server internals), operational availability (99.56% uptime 2011-2022), computational performance (~1.1M submissions/year, sub-1-second processing for ~79% of submissions), and its use in published research.
methodology: Literature/system survey methodology: review and classification of AES literature and systems by application domain; compilation of datasets and ML task tables from prior benchmark papers; in-depth technical description and empirical operational-statistics analysis (uptime equations, submission counts, waiting-time distributions 2011-2022) of the AOJ system as an illustrative case study.
findings: AESs serve 5 distinct domains beyond contests (education, recruitment, compilers, development platforms); 26+ open datasets support ML tasks from defect/clone detection to text-to-code generation; the AOJ case study shows the system achieved ~99.56% availability over 12 years, processed over 8 million submissions with growing yearly volume (~1.1M in 2022), and had ~79% of submissions evaluated within 1 second, demonstrating AES resources are both operationally reliable and valuable as large-scale real-world code datasets (e.g., feeding IBM's CodeNet and Google's AlphaCode).
limitations: Being a survey, it does not propose or evaluate a new detection/evaluation technique; the AOJ case study is a single-system example (may not generalize to all OJ platforms); coverage of newer LLM-based code-generation tools is limited since the base article predates the recent surge of large language model coding assistants.
takeaways: Useful as a catalog of datasets (e.g., CodeNet, Devign, CodeXGLUE) and ML coding tasks (vulnerability/defect detection, code repair) that could be reused for benchmarking a secure-coding tool; the AES evaluation-method formalization (test instances, verdicts, scoring) offers a template for how a code-evaluation/security-checking backend could be structured and measured for reliability and performance.
citation: Rahman, Md. Mostafizer, Yutaka Watanobe, Atsushi Shirafuji, and Mohamed Hamada. "Exploring Automated Code Evaluation Systems and Resources for Code Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey." J. ACM 37, no. 4, Article 111 (2018).

title: Secure Coding with AI – From Detection to Repair
authors: Vladislav Belozerov et al.
keywords: Secure Coding, LLMs, Vulnerability Detection, Vulnerability Repair, GPT-5, Claude, Static Analysis
objective: To evaluate the capability of modern AI coding assistants (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Claude) for automatically detecting and repairing real-world software vulnerabilities.
type: Empirical Evaluation
solution: Benchmarks multiple LLMs on real-world vulnerable code, measures vulnerability detection and repair accuracy, compares model performance, and analyzes strengths and weaknesses across vulnerability categories.
methodology: Evaluates real-world vulnerable programs using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, compares vulnerability detection and automated repair capability, and analyzes performance across vulnerability types.
findings: Modern LLMs successfully detect and repair many vulnerabilities (roughly 75–80% of detected cases), but still struggle with complex vulnerabilities and require human validation before deployment.
limitations: Focuses on evaluating existing LLMs rather than proposing a new secure coding platform. AI-generated fixes are not consistently reliable and still require expert verification.
takeaways: Validates the use of LLMs for automated vulnerability detection and repair. Supports integrating AI-based feedback into SecureCode AI while reinforcing the need for static analysis, human verification, and educational explanations.
citation: Vladislav Belozerov et al. Secure Coding with AI – From Detection to Repair. 2026.
